newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan calls for "one country, one good system".
newsitem.headline: Taiwan calls for "one country, one good system".

text.p: Taipei on Tuesday cautiously welcomed Hong Kong's return to arch rival Beijing, but said it set no precedent and Taiwan would never allow itself to be gobbled up by communist China.
Vice President Lien Chan said moments after the handover that reunification across the Taiwan strait could only come once all China -- including the mainland -- embraced democracy.
Until then things should stay unchanged -- with capitalist, democratic Taiwan in the hands of the Nationalist Republic of China and the mainland with the communist People's Republic.

"We want to maintain the status quo between the two sides of the strait. We also encourage engagement and exchanges in order to bring a better cross-strait relationship," Lien told Cable News Network.

Lien held out an olive branch on the occasion of Hong Kong's handover, inviting new Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa to visit Taiwan and saying he was willing to visit Hong Kong or anywhere else in the mainland "with no preconditions".
Beijing has said Taiwan's leaders could visit in principle, but only in their capacity as leaders of the ruling Nationalist Party, not as government officials.

Lien said Taiwan was "pleased that Hong Kong has returned to the Chinese people". But he reasserted the sovereignty of the Nationalist government, exiled on Taiwan since losing the mainland to the communists in 1949 after a civil war.
"The Republic of China is a sovereign state," he said.
"We are also a democratic country, with a government democratically elected. So we must be held accountable to the public will of the people."

Lien again rejected reunification with the mainland under the "one country, two systems" formula of local autonomy that Beijing pledges to implement in Hong Kong, saying this would be a betrayal of his democratic mandate.
Coining a new twist on Beijing's proposal, Lien said union was possible only under conditions of "one country, one good system", adding that this could only be multiparty democracy.

Lien said any reunification would be a long process that should start with restoration of bilateral contacts, which Beijing froze in mid-1995 while alleging Taipei was pushing for independence rather than reunification.
"We believe that mutual and reciprocal exchanges... will lead to mutual trust and cooperation that will in turn bring consultation and eventual political reunification," he said.
Beijing has noted the return of Hong Kong and Portuguese-run Macau's handover in 1999 would leave only Taiwan to be "reunified with the motherland".
Hong Kong has been crucial to Taiwan, acting as the main transit point for US$30 billion worth of "indirect" investment that Taiwan firms have poured into China since the 1980s.
Taiwan's government, in a formal statement of policy on Hong Kong, urged China's leaders to "consider the greater interest and fulfil their promises" to Hong Kong.
Taipei urged Beijing to adjust its "unrealistic policies and intentions toward Taiwan", a reference to Beijing's desire that Taiwan accept the communist government's sovereignty.
"I don't think anyone on this island will voluntarily accept communism as a system of society or a system of government," Vice President Lien told CNN.
